gist: A top-ten service on a firehose. Eight billion searches a day times ten keystroke requests is about 926 thousand requests per second, and every answer is the same shape: the top ten completions of a prefix. The design is one small, hot, hourly-refreshed index served from memory.

1: About 8 billion searches per day, about 10 keystroke requests per search, so about 926 thousand requests per second
Answers land in under 100 ms at p99
Only the top 10 suggestions per prefix matter
A strong candidate multiplies searches by keystrokes and asks for the latency budget instead of inventing them.
2: A prefix service answers from memory, not from the search backend
The request is tiny and cache friendly at the edge
Sketch the path: keystroke, edge, prefix index, top 10 back
A strong candidate keeps the search index out of the keystroke path.
3: The index covers about 100 million distinct queries, ranked by frequency over the last 24 hours
Trie or precomputed top-10 per prefix; only hot prefixes need their own list
Top 10 is small enough to ship as one cached payload per prefix
A strong candidate picks a structure where the answer is precomputed, not computed per keystroke.
4: About 926 thousand requests per second is the bottleneck; the index lives in memory, replicated near users
The trend refresh runs hourly: a batch job rebuilds ranks from the last 24 hours, then swaps
A stale index for minutes is fine; recomputing per request is not
The 2 percent banned list filters at index build and again at serve
A strong candidate separates the per-hour build from the per-keystroke serve.
5: The hourly rank swap bounds staleness without touching the hot path
Prefix caching at the edge absorbs repeat keystroke storms
Banned terms drop before they reach the suggestion list, at build and at serve
A strong candidate talks about swap atomicity so no request sees a half-built index.

anchors.1: Hearing the multiplier: the candidate states about 926 thousand keystroke requests per second
anchors.2: Hearing the budget: the candidate targets under 100 ms at p99
anchors.3: Hearing the shape: the candidate serves a precomputed top 10 per prefix
anchors.4: Hearing the trend: the candidate rebuilds ranks from the last 24 hours and swaps hourly
anchors.5: Hearing the index size: the candidate plans for about 100 million distinct queries in memory
anchors.6: Hearing the filter: the candidate drops the 2 percent banned queries at build time and at serve time

probes.q: The user typed three letters. Where does the answer come from, and what does it cost?
Your p99 is 120 milliseconds. What are the first two places the time goes?
One hundred million distinct queries. Do you precompute the top ten for every possible prefix? Why or why not?
A term goes viral right now. When does it appear in suggestions, and what had to run?
The rank swap happens while requests arrive. What does a request see mid-swap?
A banned term sneaks into the index overnight. When does it disappear from suggestions?
